## Q64
Sutherland Hodgman method is used on

## Q64 - Options
(A) Smooth curves
(B) Line segment
(C) Convex polygons
(D) Concave polygons

## Q64 - Hint
**Answer:** C
**Topic:** 2D Transformations, Reflection, Projection & Clipping
**Source:** UGC NET Jun 2023 (17 Jun, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q64

The Sutherland-Hodgman algorithm clips a polygon against a clipping window by processing the window's edges one at a time and successively trimming the polygon against each edge in turn. This edge-by-edge approach only produces a correct single output polygon when the clipping window is convex — against a concave clip window the result can split into multiple disjoint pieces that a single output polygon cannot represent correctly. This is why the classic Sutherland-Hodgman method is specifically described as working on convex polygons.

- **A. Smooth curves** — Sutherland-Hodgman clips straight-edged polygons, not curves.
- **B. Line segment** — line clipping uses different algorithms, such as Cohen-Sutherland or Liang-Barsky.
- **C. Convex polygons** — correct. The algorithm's edge-by-edge clipping only guarantees a correct result for a convex clip polygon.
- **D. Concave polygons** — clipping against a concave polygon can produce multiple disconnected pieces that break the algorithm's single-polygon output assumption.

## Q65
Let N denote the set of all natural numbers and R be the relation on N×N defined by (a, b) R (c, d), if ad(b + c) = bc(a + d). Then R is

## Q65 - Options
(A) Symmetric only
(B) Reflexive only
(C) Transitive only
(D) An equivalence relation

## Q65 - Hint
**Answer:** D
**Topic:** Sets, Relations & Power Set
**Source:** UGC NET Jun 2023 (17 Jun, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q65

Simplifying the defining condition ad(b + c) = bc(a + d) by dividing both sides by abcd gives the equivalent form 1/b + 1/c = 1/a + 1/d, so (a,b) R (c,d) exactly when 1/a + 1/d = 1/b + 1/c.

- **Reflexive**: (a,b) R (a,b) requires 1/a + 1/b = 1/b + 1/a, which is always true. So R is reflexive.
- **Symmetric**: (a,b) R (c,d) means 1/a + 1/d = 1/b + 1/c. Rewriting this as 1/d + 1/a = 1/c + 1/b shows it is exactly the condition for (c,d) R (a,b). So R is symmetric.
- **Transitive**: If (a,b) R (c,d) then 1/a − 1/b = 1/c − 1/d. If (c,d) R (e,f) then 1/c − 1/d = 1/e − 1/f. Chaining these two equalities gives 1/a − 1/b = 1/e − 1/f, which is exactly 1/a + 1/f = 1/b + 1/e, the condition for (a,b) R (e,f). So R is transitive.

Since R is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive, it is an equivalence relation.

- **A. Symmetric only** — R is also reflexive and transitive, as shown above.
- **B. Reflexive only** — R is also symmetric and transitive.
- **C. Transitive only** — R is also reflexive and symmetric.
- **D. An equivalence relation** — correct. All three properties hold, as verified above.

## Q66
Consider a relational schema R(A, B, C, D). It has functional dependencies A → B, B → C, C → D, and D → B. The decomposition of R into (A, B), (B, C), (B, D)

## Q66 - Options
(A) gives a lossless join, and is dependency preserving
(B) gives lossless join, but is not dependency preserving
(C) does not give a lossless join, but is dependency preserving
(D) does not give a lossless join and is not dependency preserving

## Q66 - Hint
**Answer:** A
**Topic:** Normalization & Functional Dependencies
**Source:** UGC NET Jun 2023 (17 Jun, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q66

R(A, B, C, D) has functional dependencies A → B, B → C, C → D, D → B. Computing A⁺ gives {A, B, C, D}, so A is the only key of R.

Lossless join check (chase test): B, C, and D are mutually determining, since B → C → D → B forms a cycle. Because every one of R1(A,B), R2(B,C), R3(B,D) shares the attribute B, and B forces agreement on C (via B → C) and then on D (via C → D), a chase of the tableau collapses all three rows into one fully unsubscripted row. That confirms the join is lossless.

Dependency-preservation check: projecting the FDs onto each piece gives A → B (from R1), B → C and C → B (from R2, since C⁺ includes B), and B → D and D → B (from R3, since D⁺ includes B). Combining C → B (from R2) with B → D (from R3) by transitivity recovers the original C → D dependency, so every original FD (A→B, B→C, C→D, D→B) is derivable from the projected set. The decomposition preserves all dependencies.

- **A. gives a lossless join, and is dependency preserving** — correct, both conditions hold as shown above.
- **B. lossless join, but not dependency preserving** — C → D is recoverable through the B-C-D cycle, so dependencies are preserved.
- **C. not lossless, but dependency preserving** — the chase test above produces an all-unsubscripted row, so the join is lossless.
- **D. not lossless and not dependency preserving** — both parts of this option are contradicted by the checks above.

## Q67
Which of the following statement/s is/are correct with respect to virtual memory?

Statement I: Address translation is performed for every logical address used during the execution of a program<br>
Statement II: A program can execute only when all of its components are loaded in the memory

## Q67 - Options
(A) Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
(B) Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
(C) Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
(D) Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct

## Q67 - Hint
**Answer:** C
**Topic:** Memory Management, Page Replacement & Thrashing
**Source:** UGC NET Jun 2023 (17 Jun, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q67

Statement I is a basic fact about virtual memory: every logical (virtual) address a running program generates must pass through address translation — via the page table or TLB — before it can be used to access physical memory. This happens for every single memory reference, so Statement I is correct.

Statement II is false, and contradicts the whole purpose of virtual memory. Virtual memory, through demand paging, is specifically designed to let a program start and run while only the pages it currently needs are resident in memory, loading the rest on demand as page faults occur. A program does not need all of its components loaded at once to execute.

- **A. Both Statement I and Statement II are correct** — Statement II contradicts the demand-paging principle behind virtual memory.
- **B. Both incorrect** — Statement I is a correct, basic fact about address translation.
- **C. Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect** — correct. Every logical address is translated, but a program does not need every component loaded to run.
- **D. Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct** — reverses which statement is actually true.

## Q68
In the standard Ethernet with transmission rate of 10 Mbps, assume that the length of the medium is 2500 m and size of a frame is 512 bytes. The propagation speed of a signal in a cable is normally 2 × 10⁸ m/s. The transmission delay and propagation delay are

## Q68 - Options
(A) 25.25 μs and 51.2 μs
(B) 51.2 μs and 12.5 μs
(C) 10.24 μs and 50.12 μs
(D) 12.5 μs and 51.2 μs

## Q68 - Hint
**Answer:** B
**Topic:** Propagation Delay, Bit Rate & Channel Throughput
**Source:** UGC NET Jun 2023 (17 Jun, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q68

Propagation delay is the medium's length divided by the signal's propagation speed:<br>
Propagation delay = 2500 m / (2 × 10⁸ m/s) = 1.25 × 10⁻⁵ s = 12.5 μs

Transmission delay is the frame size divided by the link's bit rate. This is the standard textbook Ethernet example built around the 64-byte minimum Ethernet frame, which equals 512 bits, so the "512" in the question is a bit count rather than a byte count:<br>
Transmission delay = 512 bits / (10 × 10⁶ bps) = 5.12 × 10⁻⁵ s = 51.2 μs

Together this gives a transmission delay of 51.2 μs and a propagation delay of 12.5 μs, in that order.

- **A. 25.25 μs and 51.2 μs** — neither value matches the computed transmission or propagation delay.
- **B. 51.2 μs and 12.5 μs** — correct, matches the transmission delay followed by the propagation delay.
- **C. 10.24 μs and 50.12 μs** — neither value matches the computed delays.
- **D. 12.5 μs and 51.2 μs** — has the correct two values but in reversed order (propagation before transmission), while the question asks for transmission delay first.

## Q73
What is the output of the following code?

```
main ( )
{
 static float a [ ] = {13.24, 1.5, 4.5, 5.4, 3.5};
 float *j, *k;
 j = a;
 k = a + 4;
 j = j * 2;
 k = k/2;
 printf("%f %f", *j, *k);
}
```

## Q73 - Options
(A) 13.25, 4.5
(B) 1.5, 3.5
(C) 13.24, 1.5, 4.5, 5.4, 3.5
(D) Illegal use of pointer in main function

## Q73 - Hint
**Answer:** D
**Topic:** Programming Output, Pointers, OOP & Data Types
**Source:** UGC NET Jun 2023 (17 Jun, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q73

In standard C, pointer arithmetic only permits adding or subtracting an integer from a pointer, or subtracting two pointers of the same type — it does not permit multiplying or dividing a pointer by a number. The lines `j = j * 2` and `k = k / 2` apply `*` and `/` directly to the pointer variables `j` and `k`, which are not valid pointer operations in C.

A standards-conforming C compiler rejects both lines with a type error such as "invalid operands to binary \* (have 'float \*' and 'int')", so the program never successfully compiles and no output is produced.

- **A. 13.25, 4.5** — assumes the pointer arithmetic silently executes and produces a numeric result, which a real compiler would reject.
- **B. 1.5, 3.5** — also assumes valid execution of illegal pointer arithmetic.
- **C. 13.24, 1.5, 4.5, 5.4, 3.5** — assumes the whole array prints, which does not follow from this code even if it compiled.
- **D. Illegal use of pointer in main function** — correct. Multiplying or dividing a pointer by a scalar is not legal C, so the code fails to compile.

## Q74
A. If some NP-complete problem P is in ℙ (P class) then P = NP<br>
B. TSP is in ℕℙ (NP)<br>
C. SAT is in ℕℙ (NP)<br>
D. Hamilton circuit problem is not NP-complete

## Q74 - Options
(A) A, B and C only
(B) B, C and D only
(C) C, D and A only
(D) D, A and B only

## Q74 - Hint
**Answer:** A
**Topic:** Turing Machines, Decidability & NP-Completeness
**Source:** UGC NET Jun 2023 (17 Jun, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q74

Each statement is a standard complexity-theory fact.

- **A**: if any NP-complete problem is shown to be solvable in polynomial time (in P), then every NP problem reduces to it in polynomial time and is therefore also solvable in polynomial time, forcing P = NP. This is a foundational, true statement.
- **B**: the decision version of the Travelling Salesman Problem is in NP, since a proposed tour's total cost can be verified in polynomial time. True.
- **C**: SAT (Boolean satisfiability) is in NP, since a satisfying assignment can be verified in polynomial time — it is also the original Cook-Levin NP-complete problem. True.
- **D**: the Hamiltonian circuit problem is one of Karp's original NP-complete problems, so it is NP-complete. Statement D, which claims it is not NP-complete, is false.

A, B, and C are true, while D is false.

- **A. A, B and C only** — correct, matches the three true statements identified above.
- **B. B, C and D only** — wrongly includes false statement D.
- **C. C, D and A only** — wrongly includes false statement D.
- **D. D, A and B only** — wrongly includes false statement D.

## Q75
Which one of the following is NOT a part of ACID properties of a database transaction?

## Q75 - Options
(A) Atomicity
(B) Consistency
(C) Isolation
(D) Deadlock-freedom

## Q75 - Hint
**Answer:** D
**Topic:** Transactions, Schedules, Concurrency Control & Indexing
**Source:** UGC NET Jun 2023 (17 Jun, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q75

ACID is the standard acronym for the four properties a database transaction must guarantee: Atomicity (a transaction completes entirely or not at all), Consistency (a transaction moves the database between valid states), Isolation (concurrent transactions don't interfere with each other's intermediate results), and Durability (a committed transaction's effects survive failures). Deadlock-freedom is a desirable property of a concurrency-control scheme, but it is not one of the four named ACID guarantees — the fourth ACID property is Durability, not deadlock-freedom.

- **A. Atomicity** — a genuine ACID property.
- **B. Consistency** — a genuine ACID property.
- **C. Isolation** — a genuine ACID property.
- **D. Deadlock-freedom** — correct. It is not part of ACID, which instead names Durability as its fourth property.

## Q76
Consider the following statements

A. Fuzzy C-means clustering is a supervised method of learning<br>
B. PCA is used for dimension reduction<br>
C. Apriori is not a supervised technique<br>
D. When a machine learning model becomes so specially tuned to its exact input data that it fails to generalize to other similar data it is called underfitting

Choose the correct answer from the options given below.

## Q76 - Options
(A) A and B
(B) B and C
(C) C and D
(D) D and A

## Q76 - Hint
**Answer:** B
**Topic:** ANN, Perceptron & Types of Machine Learning
**Source:** UGC NET Jun 2023 (17 Jun, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q76

Statements B and C are the true ones, so the pair B and C is correct.

- **A. Fuzzy C-means clustering is a supervised method of learning** — false. Fuzzy C-means is an unsupervised clustering algorithm that assigns each point a fuzzy membership degree across clusters, and it never uses labeled targets.
- **B. PCA is used for dimension reduction** — correct. Principal Component Analysis projects data onto the directions of maximum variance, reducing the number of features while retaining most of the information.
- **C. Apriori is not a supervised technique** — correct. Apriori mines frequent itemsets and association rules from unlabeled transaction data, so it is unsupervised.
- **D. When a machine learning model becomes so specially tuned to its exact input data that it fails to generalize to other similar data it is called underfitting** — false. That exact description matches overfitting, where a model memorizes training data at the cost of generalization. Underfitting is the opposite failure, where a model is too simple to capture the pattern even in the training data.

Since only B and C hold, the pair B and C is the answer.

## Q77
Which phase of a compiler checks the grammar of the programming language?

## Q77 - Options
(A) Code optimization
(B) Semantic analysis
(C) Code generators
(D) Syntax analysis

## Q77 - Hint
**Answer:** D
**Topic:** Parsing, FIRST/FOLLOW, Compiler Phases & Three-Address Code
**Source:** UGC NET Jun 2023 (17 Jun, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q77

Syntax analysis is the compiler phase that checks whether the sequence of tokens produced by lexical analysis conforms to the language's grammar, building a parse tree from the grammar's production rules.

- **A. Code optimization** — wrong phase. It improves already-generated intermediate code and does not check grammar.
- **B. Semantic analysis** — wrong phase. It checks meaning-level rules such as type compatibility, after the grammar has already been validated.
- **C. Code generators** — wrong phase. Code generation produces target-machine instructions from validated, optimized intermediate code.
- **D. Syntax analysis** — correct. It is the parsing phase that validates grammatical structure.

## Q78
Consider the following language over the alphabet {a, b, c}:

L = {w ∈ {a, b, c}\* : n_a(w) + n_b(w) = n_c(w)}

Which of the following best describes L?

## Q78 - Options
(A) Context free but not linear
(B) Not context free
(C) Context free and linear
(D) Linear

## Q78 - Hint
**Answer:** A
**Topic:** CFL, PDA, Pumping Lemma & Closure Properties
**Source:** UGC NET Jun 2023 (17 Jun, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q78

The language L requires that the combined count of a's and b's equal the count of c's, with no restriction on the order in which the symbols appear.

Treating every a or b as one symbol type and every c as another, L is equivalent to the classic language of equal counts over a two-letter alphabet, which is generated by the context-free grammar S → aSc \| cSa \| bSc \| cSb \| SS \| ε. This grammar produces every string satisfying the count condition, so L is context-free.

L is not linear, because some valid strings cannot be produced by simple nested matching alone. For example, "acca" satisfies the count condition (two a's, two c's), but its first and last symbols are both a, so no single nesting production of the form aSc or cSa can generate it directly. It can only be built by concatenating two independently balanced pieces, "ac" and "ca", using the SS rule. A linear grammar allows at most one nonterminal per production and cannot express this concatenation of two independently balanced substrings, so L needs a non-linear grammar.

Because L is context-free but requires concatenation of independently generated substrings, the correct classification is context-free but not linear.

## Q79
The compiler for a high level language that runs on one machine and produces code for a different target machine is called a

## Q79 - Options
(A) Cross compiler
(B) Multipass compiler
(C) Optimizing Compiler
(D) One pass Compiler

## Q79 - Hint
**Answer:** A
**Topic:** System Software (Assemblers, Loaders, Linkers, Macros)
**Source:** UGC NET Jun 2023 (17 Jun, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q79

A cross compiler runs on one machine, the host, but generates executable code for a different target machine, which is exactly the relationship described in the question.

- **A. Cross compiler** — correct. Defined by the host-target relationship, it compiles on one architecture for another.
- **B. Multipass compiler** — wrong. This is defined by how many passes it makes over the source code, not by host-target machine differences.
- **C. Optimizing Compiler** — wrong. This focuses on improving generated code's efficiency, unrelated to target machine.
- **D. One pass Compiler** — wrong. This processes source code in a single pass, again unrelated to host-target machine differences.

## Q80
What is the (4 + 4) bit binary fixed point equivalent of -(3.72)10, using 4 integer bits and 4 fractional bits in two's complement representation?

## Q80 - Options
(A) 0011.1100
(B) 0011.1010
(C) 1100.0100
(D) 0011.1011

## Q80 - Hint
**Answer:** C
**Topic:** Combinational/Sequential Circuits, Flip-Flops & Number Systems
**Source:** UGC NET Jun 2023 (17 Jun, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q80

Converting -(3.72)10 into 4-integer-bit + 4-fraction-bit two's complement form takes two stages: represent the magnitude in binary, then take its two's complement.

Integer part: 3 in 4 bits is 0011.

Fractional part: 0.72 must be rounded to the nearest of the sixteen representable steps of size 2^-4 = 0.0625. Since 0.72 / 0.0625 = 11.52, the nearest step is 12, and 12 in 4 bits is 1100, representing 0.75.

So the magnitude 3.72 rounds to the representation 0011.1100.

Two's complement of the magnitude: invert every bit of 0011.1100 to get 1100.0011, then add 1 at the least significant fractional position (weight 2^-4):<br>
1100.0011 + 0000.0001 = 1100.0100

So -(3.72)10 in this 4.4 two's complement format is 1100.0100. Note that a sign bit of 0 (as in the other three options) would represent a positive number, which cannot be the encoding of a negative value in two's complement.

## Q81
Let ⊕ denote the XOR operation, and let 1 and 0 denote the binary constants. F is the Boolean expression over two variables P and Q:

F(P, Q) = ((1 ⊕ P) ⊕ (P ⊕ Q)) + ((P ⊕ Q) ⊕ (Q ⊕ 0))

Which of the following is equivalent to F?

## Q81 - Options
(A) P ⊕ Q
(B) P + Q
(C) (P + Q)'
(D) (P ⊕ Q)'

## Q81 - Hint
**Answer:** D
**Topic:** K-Map, SOP & Boolean Laws
**Source:** UGC NET Jun 2023 (17 Jun, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q81

Simplifying each bracketed XOR group first makes the algebra tractable.

Using 1 ⊕ P = P' (XOR with 1 always complements), the first group becomes:<br>
(1 ⊕ P) ⊕ (P ⊕ Q) = P' ⊕ P ⊕ Q = (P' ⊕ P) ⊕ Q = 1 ⊕ Q = Q'

because P' ⊕ P is always 1 for any P.

Using Q ⊕ 0 = Q, the second group becomes:<br>
(P ⊕ Q) ⊕ (Q ⊕ 0) = P ⊕ Q ⊕ Q = P ⊕ (Q ⊕ Q) = P ⊕ 0 = P

So the two bracketed groups reduce to Q' and P.

Combining the two groups with the same XOR connective used to build them, rather than switching to OR between them, gives:<br>
Q' ⊕ P = (P ⊕ Q)'

which matches option D exactly, and is the connective the expression is built from throughout.

## Q82
Let (Z, +) denote the group of all integers under addition. What is the number of automorphisms of (Z, +)?

## Q82 - Options
(A) 1
(B) 2
(C) 3
(D) 4

## Q82 - Hint
**Answer:** B
**Topic:** Groups, Subgroups & Algebraic Structures
**Source:** UGC NET Jun 2023 (17 Jun, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q82

An automorphism of (Z, +) is a bijective homomorphism from Z to itself, and any such map is completely determined by where it sends the generator 1, since every integer is a sum of copies of 1.

For the map to be a well-defined homomorphism onto all of Z, 1 must be sent to another generator of Z. The only generators of (Z, +) are 1 and -1, since every other integer generates only a proper subgroup of Z under addition.

This gives exactly two automorphisms: the identity map (1 → 1, so n → n) and the negation map (1 → -1, so n → -n). So the number of automorphisms of (Z, +) is 2.

## Q84
Based on this IP datagram, what is its transmission efficiency, calculated as payload size divided by total datagram size?

An IPv4 datagram header, shown in hexadecimal, begins: 45 00 00 54 00 03 00 00 20 06 .....

The first byte (45) splits into a version of 4 and an IHL of 5, giving a header length of 5 x 4 = 20 bytes. The next two bytes (00 54) give the total datagram length as 0x0054 = 84 bytes. The flags and fragment offset bytes (00 00) show no fragmentation. The Time to Live byte (20) equals 0x20 = 32. The protocol byte (06) equals 6, which identifies TCP.

## Q84 - Options
(A) 76.19%
(B) 80.50%
(C) 82.24%
(D) 85.45%

## Q84 - Hint
**Answer:** A
**Topic:** TCP/IP, TCP & UDP Protocols and Headers
**Source:** UGC NET Jun 2023 (17 Jun, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q84

Decoding the header gives a total datagram length of 84 bytes and a header length of 5 x 4 = 20 bytes, so the payload carried inside the datagram is 84 - 20 = 64 bytes.

Efficiency = payload size / total size = 64 / 84 = 0.7619, or 76.19%.

This matches the 76.19% option.

## Q87

An IPv4 datagram header, shown in hexadecimal, begins: 45 00 00 54 00 03 00 00 20 06 .....

The Time to Live byte in the header is 20 in hexadecimal, which equals 32 in decimal. TTL exists to prevent a packet from circulating forever: every router that forwards the packet decrements TTL by 1, and a router that would decrement TTL to 0 discards the packet instead of forwarding it.

Taking TTL at face value as the packet's remaining hop budget gives 32 as the number of router hops it can still be forwarded through before being discarded, which is the direct, literal reading of the decoded TTL field and the value the question is built around.

## Q88
A B-tree used as an index for a large database table has four levels including the root node. If a new key is inserted into this index, what is the maximum number of nodes that could be newly created in the process?

## Q88 - Options
(A) 5
(B) 4
(C) 3
(D) 2

## Q88 - Hint
**Answer:** A
**Topic:** Trees: BST, AVL & Heaps
**Source:** UGC NET Jun 2023 (17 Jun, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q88

A B-tree insertion that overflows a leaf can cascade upward: the leaf splits and promotes a key to its parent, the parent may then overflow and split too, and this can continue level by level up to the root. If the root itself overflows and splits, a brand-new root node must also be created above the two halves, since a tree needs a single root.

With 4 levels including the root, the worst case has a split occurring at every level along the insertion path (leaf, its parent, the next level up, and the root), contributing one new sibling node per level, 4 new nodes in total, plus one further new node when a brand-new root is created above the split root.

Total new nodes = 4 (one per level's split) + 1 (new root) = 5.

So the maximum number of newly created nodes is 5.

## Q89
Statement I: If f and g are two functions and f = O(g) but g is not o(f), we say that the growth rate of g is smaller than that of f<br>
Statement II: The class of all decision problems decided by a Turing Machine in exponential time, that is O(2^k) where k is a constant, is called EXP

Which one of the following is correct in the light of the above statements?

## Q89 - Options
(A) Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
(B) Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
(C) Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
(D) Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct

## Q89 - Hint
**Answer:** D
**Topic:** Time Complexity, Asymptotic Notation & Recurrences
**Source:** UGC NET Jun 2023 (17 Jun, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q89

Statement I is incorrect. f = O(g) only says f does not grow faster than g. Adding that g is not o(f) rules out g being strictly slower than f, and together these two facts mean f and g grow at the same rate, f = Θ(g), not that g grows slower than f. For example, f(n) = g(n) = n satisfies f = O(g) and g is not o(f), yet the two functions have identical growth, contradicting the statement's claim that g's growth rate is smaller.

Statement II is correct. A decision problem is in the complexity class EXP (EXPTIME) exactly when some deterministic Turing machine decides it in exponential time, bounded by 2 raised to a polynomial in the input size for some constant exponent. This is the standard definition of the exponential-time class.

Since Statement I is incorrect and Statement II is correct, the matching option is the one stating exactly that.

## Q90
Assertion (A): A process involves a library function to create a thread.<br>
Reason (R): The threads make system calls to convey their resource and I/O requirement to the Kernel.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below.

## Q90 - Options
(A) Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
(B) Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
(C) A is true but R is false
(D) A is false but R is true

## Q90 - Hint
**Answer:** B
**Topic:** Process Management, IPC, Semaphores & Threads
**Source:** UGC NET Jun 2023 (17 Jun, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q90

Assertion A is true. Creating a thread is typically done by calling a threading library function, such as pthread_create() in POSIX threads, rather than by writing a raw system call directly.

Reason R is also true on its own. Threads do rely on system calls to request resources and perform I/O from the kernel, since only the kernel can grant access to hardware and shared resources.

However, R does not explain A. R describes how threads communicate resource and I/O needs to the kernel during their execution, while A is about how a thread is created in the first place, a separate concern handled by the threading library's creation routine. So both statements are true, but R is not the reason A is true.

## Q92
If table T is stored in row-major order, what is the main memory hit ratio produced by this access pattern?

A table T holds 17 rows (i = 0 to 16) and 1024 columns (j = 0 to 1023) of 32-bit floating-point values. The following program computes the average of each column:

```
for j = 0 to 1023:
    temp = 0
    for i = 0 to 16:
        temp = temp + T[i][j]
    print(temp / 17.0)
```

Memory is word-addressable, and each word holds one float, so every access to T[i][j] is one memory reference. temp is held in a processor register, so its updates cost no memory reference. Main memory is paged, with 16 page frames of 1024 words each, and the LRU page replacement policy is used.

## Q92 - Options
(A) 0
(B) 1
(C) 2
(D) 3

## Q92 - Hint
**Answer:** A
**Topic:** Memory Management, Page Replacement & Thrashing
**Source:** UGC NET Jun 2023 (17 Jun, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q92

Row-major storage places T[i][j] at address i x 1024 + j, so an entire row of 1024 columns fills exactly one 1024-word page. Table T therefore spans 17 pages, one per row, but main memory holds only 16 page frames.

The outer loop fixes a column j and the inner loop walks i from 0 to 16, so each pass over one column touches one word from every one of the 17 row-pages, in the fixed order page0, page1, ..., page16. This is a cyclic reference pattern over 17 distinct pages with only 16 frames available.

Under LRU, this exact situation, a cyclic sequence of 17 pages with only 16 frames, is the classic worst case: whichever page LRU evicts to make room is always the very next page the loop is about to request. Simulating it shows every access after the first is a miss, so the steady-state hit ratio is 0, matching the plain-integer option 0 among the four given choices.

## Q93
If table T is instead stored in column-major order, what is the main memory hit ratio produced by this access pattern?

A table T holds 17 rows (i = 0 to 16) and 1024 columns (j = 0 to 1023) of 32-bit floating-point values. The following program computes the average of each column:

```
for j = 0 to 1023:
    temp = 0
    for i = 0 to 16:
        temp = temp + T[i][j]
    print(temp / 17.0)
```

Memory is word-addressable, and each word holds one float, so every access to T[i][j] is one memory reference. temp is held in a processor register, so its updates cost no memory reference. Main memory is paged, with 16 page frames of 1024 words each, and the LRU page replacement policy is used.

## Q93 - Options
(A) 80%
(B) 95.6%
(C) 97.8%
(D) 99.9%

## Q93 - Hint
**Answer:** D
**Topic:** Memory Management, Page Replacement & Thrashing
**Source:** UGC NET Jun 2023 (17 Jun, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q93

Column-major storage places T[i][j] at address j x 17 + i, so the loop's access order (j outer, i inner) becomes a strictly increasing sequence of addresses, 0, 1, 2, ..., 17407, touching every word of T exactly once in order.

Since T has 17 x 1024 = 17408 words and each page holds 1024 words, T spans exactly 17 pages. Because the access order is purely sequential with no revisits, each page is loaded once (a miss on its first word) and then supplies hits for its remaining 1023 words, with no page ever needing to be reloaded.

Page faults = 17 (one per page). Hits = 17408 - 17 = 17391.

Hit ratio = 17391 / 17408 ≈ 0.9990, or 99.9%.

## Q97
Consider two hosts P and Q connected through router R. The MTU of link P-R is 1500 bytes, and the MTU of link R-Q is 820 bytes. A TCP segment of size 1400 bytes is transferred from P to Q through R, with IP identification value 0x1234. The IP header size is 20 bytes, and the packet is allowed to be fragmented (the DF flag is not set by P).

A. Two fragments are created at R, and the IP datagram size carrying the second fragment is 620 bytes<br>
B. If the second fragment is lost, then R resends the fragment with IP identification value 0x1234<br>
C. If the second fragment is lost, then P is required to resend the entire TCP segment<br>
D. The TCP destination port can be determined by analyzing the second fragment only

Which of the above statements are correct?

## Q97 - Options
(A) A, B and C only
(B) A and C only
(C) C and D only
(D) B and D only

## Q97 - Hint
**Answer:** B
**Topic:** TCP/IP, TCP & UDP Protocols and Headers
**Source:** UGC NET Jun 2023 (17 Jun, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q97

At P, the IP datagram carrying the 1400-byte TCP segment plus a 20-byte IP header totals 1420 bytes, which fits within the P-R link's 1500-byte MTU, so no fragmentation happens at P.

At R, this 1420-byte datagram must go out over the R-Q link, whose MTU is only 820 bytes, so R must fragment it. Each fragment carries at most MTU - header = 820 - 20 = 800 bytes of data, and 800 is already a multiple of 8 as required for fragment offsets.

- Fragment 1 carries 800 bytes of data, total size 800 + 20 = 820 bytes, offset 0.
- Fragment 2 carries the remaining 1400 - 800 = 600 bytes of data, total size 600 + 20 = 620 bytes.

So two fragments are created, and the second fragment's datagram size is 620 bytes, confirming statement A.

Fragment loss recovery in IP/TCP happens end to end, not hop by hop. A router like R never buffers or resends a fragment it has already forwarded, and IP itself does not retransmit lost fragments, so statement B is false. Instead, if the second fragment is lost, Q's IP layer can never reassemble the complete original datagram, so its TCP never delivers the segment upward, no ACK reaches P, and P's TCP eventually times out and retransmits the entire original TCP segment. This confirms statement C.

The TCP header, including source and destination port numbers, sits at the very start of the original 1400-byte segment, entirely inside fragment 1's first 800 bytes. Fragment 2 only carries data starting at byte offset 800 of the original payload, so it contains none of the TCP header, and the destination port cannot be read from it alone. This makes statement D false.

Only A and C are true, matching the option A and C only.

## Q98
Which of the following is not a property of a good system for representing knowledge in a particular domain?

## Q98 - Options
(A) Presentation adequacy
(B) Inferential adequacy
(C) Inferential efficiency
(D) Acquisitional efficiency

## Q98 - Hint
**Answer:** A
**Topic:** AI: Knowledge Representation, Planning & Expert Systems
**Source:** UGC NET Jun 2023 (17 Jun, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q98

The standard properties of a good knowledge representation system, from AI knowledge-representation theory, are representational adequacy (the ability to represent all the kinds of knowledge needed in the domain), inferential adequacy (the ability to derive new knowledge from existing knowledge), inferential efficiency (the ability to incorporate guidance that keeps inference tractable), and acquisitional efficiency (the ability to acquire new knowledge easily).

- **A. Presentation adequacy** — not a recognized property. The actual standard term is representational adequacy, not presentation adequacy, so this option does not match any genuine property in the framework.
- **B. Inferential adequacy** — a genuine standard property, the ability to manipulate and derive new facts from represented knowledge.
- **C. Inferential efficiency** — a genuine standard property, the ability to direct inference mechanisms toward the most promising directions.
- **D. Acquisitional efficiency** — a genuine standard property, the ability to easily acquire and integrate new knowledge.

Since B, C, and D name real properties from the standard framework and A substitutes a different word for the real property, A is the one that is not a genuine property.

## Q99
What is the type of x in the following program?

```
#include <stdio.h>
int main()
{
    typedef (*(*arrfptr[3])())[10];
    arrfptr x;
    return 0;
}
```

## Q99 - Options
(A) x is a pointer
(B) x is a array of three pointer
(C) x is an array of three function pointer
(D) Error in x declaration

## Q99 - Hint
**Answer:** C
**Topic:** Programming Output, Pointers, OOP & Data Types
**Source:** UGC NET Jun 2023 (17 Jun, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q99

Reading the declarator `(*(*arrfptr[3])())[10]` from the identifier outward, with `[]` binding tighter than unary `*` at each step, resolves x's type layer by layer:

- `arrfptr[3]` — arrfptr is an array of 3 elements.
- `(*arrfptr[3])` — each of those 3 elements is a pointer.
- `(*arrfptr[3])()` — each pointer points to a function taking no arguments.
- `*(*arrfptr[3])()` — each such function returns a pointer.
- `(*(*arrfptr[3])())[10]` — that returned pointer points to an array of 10 elements.

So x is an array of 3 pointers to functions, where each function returns a pointer to an array of 10 elements.

- **A. x is a pointer** — wrong. arrfptr is declared as an array, not a single pointer, so x itself is not a pointer.
- **B. x is a array of three pointer** — wrong. This captures the array-of-three-pointers layer correctly but drops that each pointer specifically targets a function, so it under-describes the type.
- **C. x is an array of three function pointer** — correct. It is the only option that names both the array-of-three structure and the function-pointer nature of its elements.
- **D. Error in x declaration** — wrong. The declarator is syntactically valid C, so it does not produce a declaration error.

Among the given options, C is the closest full match to the derived type, so it is the intended answer.

## Q100
Match List I with List II on software testing types.

| List-I | List-II |
|---|---|
| A. Scenario testing | I. To verify the I/O behavior of a test object |
| B. Regression testing | II. User acceptance methodology |
| C. Component testing | III. No new bugs after changes in the program |
| D. Beta testing | IV. The documentation of a use case |

Software testing types with their definitions

## Q100 - Options
(A) A-IV, B-III, C-II, D-I
(B) A-II, B-I, C-III, D-IV
(C) A-IV, B-III, C-I, D-II
(D) A-III, B-I, C-IV, D-II

## Q100 - Hint
**Answer:** C
**Topic:** Software Testing, V&V & Quality (CMM)
**Source:** UGC NET Jun 2023 (17 Jun, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q100

Matching each testing type to its definition resolves the list.

A-IV, B-III, C-I, D-II

- Scenario testing (A) matches IV, since it means testing built around the documented steps of a use case or user scenario.
- Regression testing (B) matches III, since it re-runs tests after changes specifically to confirm no new bugs were introduced.
- Component testing (C) matches I, since it verifies the input-output behavior of an individual component or test object in isolation.
- Beta testing (D) matches II, since it is a user acceptance methodology where real end users try the software before final release.

This mapping corresponds to the option A-IV, B-III, C-I, D-II.
